l: clinical decision support, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: Clinical decision support is the application focus of a proposed framework for AI-generated recommendations. The framework integrates literature- and practice-derived data into machine-interpretable knowledge bases, adds evidence retrieval, citation, and forensic audit logging, and aims to provide workflow-fitting guidance that clinicians can inspect. Its central adoption constraints are transparency, verifiability, and accountability.

l: retrieval-augmented generation, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: Retrieval-augmented generation is a technology and method for citation-assisted generation: it searches curated medical literature and databases, processes retrieved texts with patient data, and synthesizes recommendations or summaries. Its central purpose is source verification, linking each generated claim to identifiable clinical guidelines, peer-reviewed sources, or specific repository documents. In the proposed framework, it is constrained to verified retrieved sources and records retrieval and decision pathways through audit logging. Citation fidelity remains a feasibility challenge.

l: data provenance, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: Data provenance is a core architectural constraint in a proposed source-verified clinical AI framework integrated with retrieval-augmented generation. It supplies explicit metadata on the origins and handling of clinical knowledge and system outputs. The framework records data, references, retrieval steps, and decision pathways to make AI suggestions traceable, auditable, and verifiable. Its forensic audit logging identifies authors, dates, source types, guideline sections, and versions, enabling evidence verification and retrospective auditing of recommendations.

l: auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: This is a conceptual, future-oriented framework for auditable and source-verified AI-based clinical decision support. Grounded in evidence-based medicine, data provenance, trustworthy AI, and verified sources for factual claims, it synthesizes existing technical approaches rather than presenting a new algorithm or prototype. Its central aim is to improve traceability, clinician trust, and regulatory readiness while promoting transparency, reliability, user control, source verification, auditability, and safety monitoring. The design begins with a Data and Knowledge Layer: a curated, comprehensive, up-to-date medical knowledge base with explicit provenance metadata. A Retrieval and Reasoning Engine then constrains reasoning to verified retrieved sources, anchoring probabilistic model behavior to a deterministic evidence base. It attaches reference IDs to answer points and addresses citation fidelity. Finally, a User Interface with Audit Logging presents clinician-centered annotated clinical guidelines and records retrieval, reasoning, and decision pathways in tamper-evident, inspectable logs for accountability, investigation, and monitoring. The framework’s main unresolved issue is knowledge-base governance and updating; it also identifies bias, latency, usability, privacy, and regulatory alignment as concerns. It has not been implemented, tested, or empirically validated, so its practical effectiveness is unknown. Its planned path forward includes implementation, clinical integration, staged simulation studies, clinician-centered user research, broader evaluations, and continuous monitoring.

l: trustworthy AI, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: Trustworthy AI is one of the principles underlying the proposed framework for auditable and source-verified clinical decision support.

s: Evidence-Based Medicine is a medical decision-making theory established in the 1990s. It requires therapeutic judgments to combine personal competence with the most reliable external evidence, making source verification foundational to clinical decision support and reflected in systems deriving recommendations from curated clinical guidelines.

l: curated medical knowledge base, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance

It integrates structured and unstructured sources, including guidelines, drug interaction databases, PubMed abstracts, and textbooks, with explicit provenance, GRADE evidence grades, SNOMED-CT and UMLS terminology, bias-auditing information, and update records. It supports retrieval-augmented reasoning and forensic audit logging, though governance and updating remain feasibility challenges.

l: RAG architectures, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: RAG architectures are systems for clinical AI decision support that map and disambiguate clinical language, retrieve evidence, and generate patient-specific recommendations linked to clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources. Their central challenge is citation fidelity: generated citations can be unsupported or misattributed. The framework addresses this risk through confidence scoring, ensemble retrieval, post-hoc verification, forensic audit logging, and future citation-verification and mitigation modules.

l: tamper-evident audit logging mechanism, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
s: The tamper-evident audit logging mechanism is a secure audit trail within the proposed framework. It records system inputs, patient-data elements as cryptographic hashes, retrieved evidence and document identifiers, inference-chain information, final-output identifiers, timestamps, and user and session identifiers. By preserving the retrieval and decision pathway, it enables retrospective reconstruction of what information the AI used and how a recommendation or final suggestion was derived. It supports transparency, integrity, traceability, accountability, auditing, and review by clinicians, hospitals, regulators, or auditors, and can help track performance and investigate adverse events. Extensive logging may also create latency, usability, privacy, and security concerns.

The account begins with expected clinical benefits, contrasts earlier inspectable rule-based systems with current risks such as probabilistic reasoning, hallucination, citation instability, and transparency needs, and concludes with an auditable, source-verified framework.

The framework presents this information without default exposure to raw model outputs or complex probability scores, while preserving processing logs for deeper inspection. It unfolds from its role in trust and adoption, through transparency mechanisms, to evidence review and forensic audit logging.

It requires each AI-generated claim to trace to an authoritative medical source, with exact citations to retrieved references. It unfolds by attaching explicit references to recommendations, letting clinicians inspect guideline excerpts or abstracts, and checking claims against cited passages. It connects recommendations to evidence and aims to reduce unsupported outputs, but cannot guarantee accuracy if the underlying evidence is flawed, outdated, or biased.

l: A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: This survey, “A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models,” by Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Zheng Yuan, Huachi Zhou, Zijin Hong, Hao Chen, Yilin Xiao, Chuang Zhou, Junnan Dong, Yi Chang, and Xiao Huang, examines GraphRAG for improving LLM performance in specialized, knowledge-intensive domains. It begins by noting that LLMs, including the GPT series, can lack domain expertise and struggle with complex queries, dispersed knowledge, limited context windows, efficiency, and scalability. Traditional RAG supplies external knowledge through chunking, embeddings, vector databases, retrieval methods such as k-nearest neighbor retrieval and BM25, and prompt integration, but remains limited in contextual coherence and multi-step reasoning. The survey presents GraphRAG as an extension of RAG that uses graphs either as knowledge carriers, knowledge indexes, or both. Its central taxonomy distinguishes Knowledge-based GraphRAG, which uses explicit knowledge graphs for structured retrieval and multi-hop reasoning; Index-based GraphRAG, which uses graphs to retrieve relevant raw text chunks; and Hybrid GraphRAG, which links graph representations with source text to combine logical reasoning and detailed context. GraphRAG is presented as improving relationship modeling, context-preserving retrieval, flexible source integration, interpretability, updating, and coherent generation. It then explains GraphRAG’s mechanisms. Knowledge organization turns text corpora, documents, search results, and interaction data into graph-supported resources. Retrieval includes query and graph preprocessing, matching, pruning, semantic similarity, logical reasoning, GNNs, LLMs, reinforcement learning, and multi-round, post-retrieval, or hybrid strategies. Knowledge integration injects retrieved nodes, paths, subgraphs, and documents into prompts or training objectives through fine-tuning and in-context learning, with graph-enhanced Chain-of-Thought, collaborative knowledge graph refinement, domain-specific models, and multi-round integration. The survey also reviews datasets, applications, and projects including SubgraphRAG, StructRAG, KG-RAG, MedGraphRAG, Microsoft GraphRAG, Nano-GraphRAG, Azure GraphRAG, Fast GraphRAG, LightRAG, and Medical GraphRAG. It closes by emphasizing unresolved issues: knowledge quality and conflict, incomplete or inconsistent retrieval, hallucination, privacy, security, dense graphs, computational overhead, and large-scale scalability. Proposed opportunities include uncertainty modeling, governance, privacy-preserving computation, distillation, pruning, compression, scalable graph algorithms, and hardware acceleration.

s: A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models is a survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation focused on Customized Large Language Models. It presents this subject as its central concern and is authored by Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Zheng Yuan, Huachi Zhou, Zijin Hong, Hao Chen, Yilin Xiao, Chuang Zhou, Junnan Dong, Yi Chang, and Xiao Huang.

l: GraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: GraphRAG, or Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, is a graph-based subclass of retrieval-augmented generation and a paradigm for domain-specific LLM applications. It organizes external, structured and unstructured knowledge into graph-based resources, then retrieves and integrates relevant knowledge to enrich large language models with organized background knowledge and improved contextual reasoning. Its central value is support for complex and multi-hop reasoning: rather than relying only on conventional retrieval, it can retrieve subgraphs centered on topics or anchor entities, use connected paths, and prune irrelevant information to produce accurate, logically coherent generation. The approach unfolds through knowledge organization, retrieval, and integration. In planning and indexing, it draws concepts and element instances from source documents, summarizes elements, groups them into communities with community-detection algorithms such as Leiden, and creates community summaries. This yields a hierarchical, comprehensive knowledge base, reflecting inspiration from earlier tree-like indexing while using graph structure. For a query, retrieval can obtain node-, path-, or subgraph-level factual knowledge, including community summaries for global inquiries. It then combines community answers into a global answer; it is described as outperforming traditional retrieval on global questions in breadth and diversity of insights. Retrieved graph knowledge is integrated into LLMs through fine-tuning, in-context learning, graph-enhanced reasoning, or knowledge graph refinement. GraphRAG includes Knowledge-based, Index-based, and Hybrid GraphRAG, and is also presented through the paradigms Graphs for Knowledge Indexing, Graphs as Knowledge Carrier, and Hybrid GraphRAG. It supports applications including healthcare, finance, education, legislation, scientific research, and other natural language processing tasks. Its effectiveness depends on external-knowledge quality, while knowledge conflict, data privacy, and efficiency are critical limitations; reconciliation, consistency management, and alignment between external knowledge and generated outputs are required.

l: large language model, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Large language models demonstrate remarkable natural language processing capabilities across a wide range of tasks, including text comprehension, question answering, and content generation. They perform strongly on general tasks, but specialized applications remain challenging: their broad pre-trained knowledge can be shallow in specialized fields, and they may have limited domain-specific accuracy, logical consistency, and handling of context-dependent interpretations. Knowledge limitations, reasoning complexity, context sensitivity, fixed context windows, and difficulty capturing long-range dependencies can reduce effectiveness, particularly when information is excessive or widely distributed. In GraphRAG, a large language model is the system that receives retrieved knowledge and combines it with inherent knowledge for reasoning and response generation. It functions as an intelligent agent for graph-based organization and integration: generating summaries, extracting facts, constructing knowledge graphs, supporting retrieval and planning, producing contextual embeddings and query expansions, interpreting graph content, identifying retrieval paths, and synthesizing multiple sources. It may be prompted with retrieved information to build more credible reasoning chains, assess content, decide when retrieval is needed, and generate labels or memory. GraphRAG enhances the model with structured context, runtime prompt augmentation, graph-based retrieval, and domain-specific background knowledge, improving complex-query performance. The model can be adapted through fine-tuning, in-context learning, or combination with graph and domain-specific models. However, it is not inherently equipped for graph-structured data, and large graph problems remain difficult because of input-length limits. Future improvement focuses on aligning external structured knowledge with learned representations through knowledge distillation, fine-tuning, cross-modal integration, uncertainty modeling, and probabilistic reasoning.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a framework and approach for customizing large language models for specific or professional fields without changing their architecture or parameters. It integrates pre-constructed external knowledge bases, enabling real-time access to domain-specific expertise during inference. Its traditional pipeline unfolds through knowledge preparation, retrieval of relevant external information, and integration of that information to prompt generation. By grounding responses in retrieved knowledge, it aims to make content more substantiated and accurate and to reduce hallucinations and inconsistencies. Its basic pipeline nevertheless faces challenges in complex query understanding, distributed knowledge integration, context limits, and efficiency.

s: Domain expertise is difficult for large language models because their pre-trained knowledge is broad but shallow and may not reflect current professional standards and practices.

l: RAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: RAG is a promising solution that enhances LLMs’ domain-specific capabilities by integrating external knowledge bases. Traditional RAG is based on flat text retrieval: it organizes document collections into text chunks in vector databases and retrieves chunks through semantic similarity, KNN, TF-IDF, or BM25. Its core components are knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, and knowledge integration. Traditional systems struggle with structured knowledge, complex professional and multi-hop queries, distributed sources, long-distance dependencies, excessive retrieved content, large-scale unstructured sources, and efficiency and contextual coherence. These limitations motivate GraphRAG, particularly for structured knowledge and more effective integration across sources.

l: flat text retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Flat text retrieval is the basis of traditional RAG systems and is associated with challenges in complex query understanding, distributed knowledge integration, and system efficiency at scale.

l: complex query understanding, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a challenge for retrieval-augmented generation [in specialized domains] Complex query understanding is a major challenge for retrieval-augmented generation in specialized domains. Traditional keyword and vector-similarity retrieval may miss semantic nuances, intermediate concepts, and the multi-step reasoning needed to connect related concepts.

l: graph-structured knowledge representation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Graph-structured knowledge representation, a key GraphRAG innovation, explicitly captures entity relationships and domain hierarchies.

l: graph-based retrieval techniques, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Graph-based retrieval techniques, a key GraphRAG innovation, preserve context in knowledge retrieval and enable multihop reasoning.

l: multi-hop reasoning, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Multi-hop reasoning is an ability in LLM performance that follows connected relationships across multiple nodes, requiring subgraphs, intermediate steps, relational information, and effective prompt structure. In GraphRAG, graph-based retrieval navigates entity-relation paths while preserving context, unlike traditional RAG’s locally similar chunks. Its performance on complex questions can be improved through multi-round integration and graph-enhanced Chain-of-Thought.

l: structure-aware knowledge integration algorithms, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Structure-aware knowledge integration algorithms are a key innovation of GraphRAG, leveraging retrieved knowledge to support accurate, logically coherent generation by large language models.

l: knowledge graphs, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge graphs are structured representations of entities, concepts, relations, and facts, often modeling domain concepts as nodes and semantic relationships as edges. They represent hierarchical relationships and complex knowledge dependencies, and can be extracted from corpora or drawn from domain-specific and general-purpose resources. In GraphRAG, they supply fine-grained information and relevant subgraphs for retrieval, logic-guided chain retrieval, reasoning-path planning, and multi-step reasoning over long spans. Combined with structured and unstructured sources, they support contextual understanding, graph construction, question answering, dialog generation, decision support, response verification, and factual refinement that can reduce hallucination. Their usefulness depends on timeliness, accuracy, completeness, and correct intermediate processing, while high-quality graph shortages and cross-domain ontology inconsistency remain limitations. Their deployment also raises privacy-preserving integration needs and requires efficient matching, traversal, reasoning, and specialized hardware for large-scale graphs.

l: GPT series, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a large language models The GPT series is identified as an example of large language models that demonstrate strong performance in text comprehension, question answering, and content generation. It is also associated with limitations in knowledge-intensive and specialized-domain tasks.

l: knowledge-intensive tasks, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge-intensive tasks expose language-model weaknesses because specialized information, multi-step reasoning, and domain constraints require expertise rarely seen in pre-training.

l: fine-tuning, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Fine-tuning is a strategy and knowledge integration method for adapting open-source large language models to specialized or private domains using specialized datasets while fixing most pre-trained parameters and adding limited parameters. It directly injects graph-retrieved information through LoRA-based and other data-efficient strategies, training with node-, path-, or subgraph-level knowledge and supporting GraphRAG alignment. It permanently integrates domain-specific knowledge, reducing reliance on extensive text retrieval and potentially improving speed and costs. However, distribution gaps and conflicting updates can harm existing understanding through catastrophic forgetting, and fine-tuning may require hundreds of gigabytes of memory.

l: catastrophic forgetting, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a risk of supervised fine-tuning [during knowledge updates] Catastrophic forgetting is identified as a possible consequence of using supervised fine-tuning to update knowledge, especially when new information conflicts with pre-existing information. Such updating can also cause new hallucinations.

l: knowledge retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge retrieval is an information-gathering stage in the traditional RAG pipeline and a retrieval process within GraphRAG. It accesses organized repositories, graph databases, or external sources to extract background knowledge and select pertinent documents for a query, improving generated outputs. It begins with query preprocessing, then matches relevant content, and ends with knowledge pruning. Current methods include K-nearest neighbor retrieval, term frequency-inverse document frequency, and Best Matching 25. Its outputs are synthesized into prompts or used as training information during knowledge integration. Unlike traditional RAG, GraphRAG also considers graph structure, logical coherence, and relationships among retrieved knowledge.

l: domain knowledge, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_distributed_across multiple documents [including textbooks, research papers, industry reports, technical manuals, and maintenance logs] Domain knowledge is distributed across sources such as textbooks, research papers, industry reports, technical manuals, and maintenance logs, which may vary in quality, accuracy, and completeness. Chunking these sources for retrieval can remove context and weaken connections among related knowledge points.

l: context window, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: constrains large language models [with a fixed capacity typically ranging from 2K to 32K tokens] The fixed context window of large language models limits the amount of retrieved domain knowledge that can be processed at once. Information beyond the window may be truncated or summarized, causing the loss of semantic units, logical flow, and long-range dependencies.

l: system efficiency and scalability, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a challenge for retrieval-augmented generation [across preprocessing, indexing, retrieval, and generation] System efficiency and scalability are constrained across the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, from preprocessing and indexing to retrieval and generation. Large knowledge bases can increase computation and latency, while retrieval quality and accuracy may decline as the knowledge base grows.

l: Knowledge-based GraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge-based GraphRAG transforms unstructured document chunks into summarized knowledge carried in explicit knowledge graphs, representing domain concepts as nodes and semantic relationships as edges. It unifies atomic facts or community summaries in a knowledge base, enabling logic-guided retrieval, entity or relation resolution, and coherent multi-step reasoning.

l: Index-based GraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Index-based GraphRAG is a graph-based indexing architecture for chunked raw text that retains the original textual form. It organizes passages through semantic, keyword, or domain-specific connections, including links from high-level topics to facts and text. These graph connections improve lookup, retrieval efficiency, and navigation: relevant topic or passage nodes are found, their raw text chunks are retrieved, and the chunks are supplied for language-model knowledge injection and subsequent processing.

l: Hybrid GraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Hybrid GraphRAG is a GraphRAG approach and one of three survey categories. It combines Knowledge-based GraphRAG and Index-based GraphRAG, using graph structures as knowledge carriers and indexing tools. It links key-information graph nodes to raw text chunks, preserving detailed context while supporting knowledge graphs and logical reasoning for complex reasoning.

l: LightRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: LightRAG is an open-source, lightweight GraphRAG implementation for cross-domain graph construction and question answering, supporting UltraDomain while reducing complexity and resource needs for constrained environments.

l: SubgraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a GraphRAG model [general domain] SubgraphRAG is a general-domain GraphRAG model designed for question answering. It uses Freebase and is evaluated on WebQSP and CWQ.

l: MedGraphRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: MedGraphRAG is a GraphRAG healthcare and medical question-answering system. It builds a medical triple knowledge graph from credible sources and controlled vocabularies, uses MultiMedQA, DiverseHealth, MedC-K, and UMLS, and integrates multimodal data for personalized healthcare solutions.

l: StructRAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a GraphRAG model [general domain] StructRAG is a general-domain model for question answering that handles broad contextual understanding through structured representations. It is associated with the Loong dataset and podcast transcripts.

l: WebQSP, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: WebQSP is a question answering dataset of 4,737 natural-language questions over a knowledge graph containing 164.6 million facts and 24.9 million entities; questions chiefly use single-fact retrieval, with two-hop aggregation and constraint reasoning also represented.

l: Graphs as Knowledge Carrier, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Graphs as Knowledge Carrier is one of two primary paradigms for structured knowledge organization in GraphRAG systems, extracting summarized knowledge from text chunks into a unified knowledge base for retrieval, reasoning, and resolving linguistic variation.

l: index graphs, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Index graphs are a structured knowledge organization paradigm in GraphRAG systems. They organize raw text chunks or other retrievable items as nodes linked by query-oriented, semantic, keyword, or domain-specific relationships, localizing relevant knowledge and retrieving text for language-model-based answering.

l: structured knowledge, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Structured knowledge is examined as a central concern of GraphRAG, which is introduced to address traditional RAG systems’ limitations in handling it.

l: knowledge base, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A knowledge base is a structured source of factual information for retrieval. Organized as a graph of entities, relations, and triples, it supports finding relevant facts, connected components, and subgraphs. It can grow through public updates, authoritative databases, expert validation, inferred relationships, and multimodal information, requiring validation for errors, gaps, and consistency. In GraphRAG, integrated sources, ontologies, and schemas are hierarchically organized into communities and reports for retrieval.

l: knowledge organization, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge organization is a pre-retrieval, two-step process that prepares external knowledge bases for rapid, relevant retrieval. It is examined through knowledge carrier graphs and index graphs. In traditional RAG, it divides large corpora into manageable text chunks, transforms them into embeddings with an embedding model, and stores them in a vector database for distance-based semantic search; it also optimizes granularity through chunking and indexing through metadata and hierarchical indexing. In GraphRAG, it constructs more expressive graph structures, then retrieves and integrates query-relevant information, aiming to reduce irrelevant results, missing context, information overload, and knowledge conflicts.

l: retrieval techniques, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Retrieval techniques are methods for extracting query-relevant factual information from structured knowledge bases; in a traditional RAG pipeline, they select external information to improve generated outputs through expansion, re-ranking, timing, filtering, APIs, and need determination.

l: knowledge integration, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge integration is the synthesis phase after knowledge retrieval: it incorporates retrieved knowledge into large language models, combines retrieved information with the input query and inherent knowledge, and generates coherent, accurate final responses. Its central concern is effective incorporation of useful knowledge, including domain-specific and graph-structured information, while preserving valuable subgraph context without redundancy or overemphasis. It primarily unfolds by synthesizing retrieved documents into cohesive prompts and setting training goals, using fine-tuning or in-context learning. Filtering, self-reflection, selective retrieval, compression, pre-encoding, caching, and parallel retrieval and generation can improve quality and efficiency. Its design must also address computational overhead and the challenges of large-scale graphs.

l: Benchmark Datasets, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a evaluation resources [for GraphRAG and KGQA systems] Benchmark Datasets are categorized into simple question answering, multi-hop reasoning, large-scale complex QA, domain-specific QA, and tailored GraphRAG benchmarks. They are used to evaluate retrieval, semantic parsing, logical reasoning, knowledge validation, graph construction, contextual summarization, and generation.

l: GraphRAG survey, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: GraphRAG survey is a comprehensive analysis of GraphRAG, organized into seven main sections that move from foundational concepts to practical implementation. It establishes a foundational framework, presents taxonomy and mechanisms, reviews open-source projects and benchmark datasets, and offers domain-specific case studies and implementation examples for production deployment. It also examines challenges in knowledge quality, retrieval efficiency, system generalization, and security, then identifies future research directions. It aims to advance existing GraphRAG surveys through a more systematic, practical review.

l: knowledge quality, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge quality is identified as one of the dimensions in which GraphRAG challenges and potential solutions are analyzed. Knowledge quality is essential to GraphRAG effectiveness. It can be improved through systematic organization, automated refinement, continuous expansion, multimodal integration, anomaly detection, knowledge base completion, and alignment.

l: retrieval efficiency, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Retrieval efficiency is identified as one of the dimensions in which GraphRAG challenges and potential solutions are analyzed.

l: system generalization, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: System generalization is identified as one of the dimensions in which GraphRAG challenges and potential solutions are analyzed.

l: security, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Security is identified as one of the dimensions in which GraphRAG challenges and potential solutions are analyzed.

l: traditional RAG pipeline, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Traditional RAG pipeline is a process with three core components: knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, and knowledge integration. It begins by preparing external knowledge, then selects or retrieves relevant content, and ends by using that content to support generated responses.

l: vector database, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A vector database stores embeddings linked to original text chunks and retrieves them efficiently through distance-based semantic search. Its flat organization supports lookup but can struggle to capture multi-hop relationships, hierarchies, and connections across distributed domain knowledge.

l: graph database, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A graph database stores and retrieves connected knowledge through graph structures. It supports relationship-based queries and graph traversal, with dense information as a retrieval target. It can scale and update through added nodes or edges, then is processed into retrieval indexes using dense entity, relation, and triple representations, structural features, or rule banks.

l: subgraph, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A subgraph is a relevant portion of a graph retrieved for a query. GraphRAG uses subgraph retrieval and pruning to focus generation on connected knowledge while removing irrelevant information. A subgraph is a retrieved portion of the graph containing knowledge relevant to a query. An ideal subgraph covers source and target entities, has strong contextual relevance, and contains little redundant information.

l: graph structure, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: represents relation [including hierarchies, associations, and multi-hop relationships] A graph structure models dependencies and relationships among knowledge pieces. It can represent hierarchies, associations, and multi-hop relationships, enabling richer semantic context, relationship-based search, and traceable reasoning paths.

l: vector similarity retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: retrieves text chunk [by semantic similarity] Vector similarity retrieval selects text chunks according to semantic similarity between a query and stored representations. It may retrieve excessive or disconnected content and has difficulty establishing clear long-distance connections among separate pieces of knowledge.

l: information retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a graph-based retrieval capability Knowledge retrieval in GraphRAG uses the connections and hierarchical organization of graph knowledge bases rather than examining isolated information pieces. Community summaries provide local perspectives that are synthesized into broader answers, improving the breadth and diversity of insights for global questions.

l: external knowledge, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: includes multimodal information [beyond traditional text-based knowledge] External knowledge is the foundation of GraphRAG effectiveness and must be organized, refined, expanded, and validated. It may be enriched through web crawling, authoritative database APIs, expert feedback, machine learning, and multimodal information such as images and videos.

l: text corpus, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A text corpus is split into manageable units during knowledge organization. Its contents can also be pre-encoded or indexed to support efficient retrieval.

l: text chunk, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A text chunk is a manageable segment or detailed source passage from a larger corpus used in traditional RAG knowledge organization. It is transformed into an embedding, stored for retrieval, and may carry metadata for filtering and re-ranking. In graph-based organization, it can be indexed as a node or linked to summarized knowledge, enabling retrieval of detailed context. Chunk size matters: overly fine chunks can lose semantic integrity, while overly coarse ones can add redundancy.

l: embedding model, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Embedding model serves as vector-database keys, represents text chunks semantically, and enables neighbor identification before BM25 re-ranking.

l: query, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A query provides the information need that directs retrieval and generation. Traditional RAG matches it mainly with semantically similar chunks, while GraphRAG can use topics, entities, relationships, and graph paths to retrieve more structurally relevant knowledge. The query is transformed into a structured representation through vectorization or key term extraction. Its representation is compared with graph indexes during matching.

l: retrieval module, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: The retrieval module searches organized knowledge for information relevant to a query. In traditional RAG it may search large volumes of unstructured text and return unnecessary content, while GraphRAG can use structural relationships to improve relevance and efficiency.

l: K-nearest neighbor retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: calculates L2 distance [to extract approximate relevant neighbors] K-nearest neighbor retrieval is used to retrieve relevant content from organized knowledge repositories. RETRO applies it by calculating L2 distance to extract approximate relevant neighbors from a key-value database.

l: Best Matching 25, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Best matching 25, also called BM25, is a retrieval method used to identify relevant content. It can be combined with query expansion, re-ranking, or sentence-transformer representations to improve accuracy and computational efficiency.

l: GraphRAG knowledge carrier, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a graph [that carries explicit knowledge representation] A GraphRAG knowledge carrier is a graph used to represent knowledge explicitly. It models entities and their relations so that GraphRAG can retrieve connected information and support reasoning across multiple nodes.

l: entity, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Entities are graph elements that can be transformed into dense vectors and used as retrieval anchors. They may also serve as source, target, or seed entities during subgraph and path retrieval.

l: relation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A relation connects entities or concepts in a graph and expresses how pieces of knowledge depend on or associate with one another. Relations enable GraphRAG to discover connected knowledge, conduct multi-hop reasoning, and expose reasoning paths. Relations are graph elements represented during preprocessing and considered in retrieval. Relational embeddings can be used to prune information that is less pertinent to a query.

l: node, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A node represents an entity, concept, topic, or other unit of knowledge in a graph. GraphRAG can retrieve and traverse nodes, add new nodes when knowledge is updated, and use topic nodes or anchor entities to guide retrieval.

l: knowledge carrier, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A knowledge carrier stores condensed knowledge from raw corpora, including atomic facts and community summaries, and is integrated into a knowledge base to support retrieval and reasoning.

l: Graphs for Knowledge Indexing, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Graphs for Knowledge Indexing is an index graph construction paradigm that represents text chunks as nodes and query-oriented relationships as edges, enabling multi-level summarization, localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval.

l: GraphRAG with KGs constructed from corpus, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: transforms raw text chunk [into structured graph representations] GraphRAG with KGs constructed from corpus transforms unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs, often using Open Information Extraction techniques. It faces challenges involving domain-specific ontologies, graph complexity, information granularity, computational efficiency, and the cost of language-model-based summarization.

l: GraphRAG with existing KGs, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: uses knowledge graph [well-established domain-specific or general-purpose graphs] GraphRAG with existing KGs uses established domain-specific or general-purpose knowledge graphs. Its central challenge is dynamically planning and retrieving relevant reasoning paths or subgraphs while maintaining relevance, conciseness, and recall despite graph incompleteness.

l: KG-RAG, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: uses SPOKE [specialized biomedical knowledge graph] KG-RAG is a biomedical question-answering system that uses the SPOKE knowledge graph and is evaluated on MCQ. The unit describes it as linking symptoms, diseases, and treatments to provide accurate and interpretable insights.

l: graph preprocessing, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Graph preprocessing is a stage for graph databases that transforms graph elements into dense vector retrieval anchors, using pre-trained language models, graph neural networks for structural features, and rule mining for searchable rule banks.

l: query preprocessing, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Query preprocessing transforms an input question through vectorization or key term extraction into a structured representation that serves as a search index for later retrieval.

l: matching, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Matching is a retrieval stage connecting query representations with graph indices, comparing preprocessed queries by semantic similarity and structural relationships to retrieve relevant components and highly relevant subgraphs.

l: knowledge pruning, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Knowledge pruning is a refinement stage after initial retrieval that removes irrelevant or noisy information, consolidates related fragments, and can summarize complex graph knowledge.

l: knowledge summarization, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: facilitates knowledge synthesis [for LLM generation] Knowledge summarization produces a distilled account of retrieved graph knowledge. It is intended to help large language models synthesize context and generate more accurate and meaningful responses.

l: graph neural network, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: A graph neural network can be applied to a graph database to extract high-level structural features. Its message-passing mechanism aggregates information from neighboring nodes to update node representations.

l: rule mining, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Rule mining can generate rule banks that act as rich, searchable indexes of graph knowledge. It is also used in logical reasoning-based retrieval to uncover information not explicitly present in the data.

l: semantic similarity-based retriever, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a retrieval technique [measures similarity between queries and the knowledge base] The semantic similarity-based retriever measures similarity between a query and knowledge-base content in discrete linguistic or continuous vector space. It includes string matching and embedding space modeling, but may underuse graph structure.

l: string matching, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: String matching is a retrieval technique based on exact, substring, regular-expression, or phrase matching; it identifies relevant graph nodes and edges simply for well-defined vocabularies, but cannot handle terminology variations, synonyms, or contextual nuance.

l: embedding space modeling, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Embedding space modeling maps queries and graph entities into a continuous vector space for contextual and conceptual connections. Using TF-IDF, Word2Vec, and GloVe, it retrieves semantically relevant information without exact matches, but underutilizes graph structure.

l: logical reasoning-based retriever, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Logical reasoning-based retriever uses symbolic reasoning, logical rules, constraints, rule mining, inductive logic programming, and constraint satisfaction to deduce and extract relevant information from graph knowledge bases.

l: GNN-based retriever, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: GNN-based retriever uses trained GNN encoders to represent graph knowledge-base nodes, then retrieves knowledge by comparing node similarities that capture semantic meaning and structural relationships.

l: LLM-based retriever, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: LLM-based retriever uses large language models to interpret queries, expand or disambiguate them, identify key subgraphs, and synthesize candidate information. Guided by prompts without retriever training, it may require training when results support model reflection or fine-tuning.

l: reinforcement learning-based retriever, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: uses reinforcement learning [for sequential graph traversal] The reinforcement learning-based retriever treats graph retrieval as sequential decision-making. It learns to traverse or sample reasoning chains in search of concise, relevant subgraphs, using methods such as Deep Q-Networks, policy gradients, and actor-critic approaches.

l: reinforcement learning, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Reinforcement learning is an adaptive retrieval strategy: an agent learns from environmental feedback and experience, using Deep Q-Networks, Policy Gradients, or Actor-Critic to refine retrieval, sample reasoning chains, and improve graph traversal decisions.

l: multi-round retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: uses user feedback [to refine retrieval dynamically] Multi-round retrieval incorporates contextual information and user feedback to refine retrieval dynamically. It aims to align the retriever more closely with specific use cases and changing user intent.

l: post-retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Post-retrieval conducts retrieval after generation to evaluate generated answers for faithfulness and accuracy, guiding the large language model to rethink and correct responses.

l: hybrid retrieval, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: combines graph database [with other data formats] Hybrid retrieval combines graphs with other data formats or retrieval sources to complement their strengths and weaknesses. It can jointly use knowledge graphs, vector databases, text documents, online web resources, and other sources.

l: in-context learning, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: In-context learning is an indirect knowledge integration strategy for closed-source LLMs, proceeding by first choosing a prompt format, then optimizing responses using retrieved content and questions.

l: prompt, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: influences large language model [through its format] A prompt joins retrieved content with questions to support response generation or further optimization. Prompt format is important because large language models are sensitive to factors such as the order of examples.

l: node-level knowledge, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Individual graph-node knowledge supports domain-specific comprehension through instruction tuning, focusing on nodes linked to documents; it uses node and neighboring text for prediction and distills long texts into embeddings.

l: path-level knowledge, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Path-level knowledge captures connections and node sequences, enhances reasoning through evidence-based support, and guides large language models via transitional relationships, training objectives, and filtering of noisy paths.

l: subgraph-level knowledge, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Subgraph-level knowledge is larger, irregular multi-node structure; it is integrated by compression, transformation, adapted transformer representation, or direct prompting.

l: graph-enhanced Chain-of-Thought, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a in-context learning technique [for knowledge integration] Graph-enhanced Chain-of-Thought uses graph structures to improve the reasoning process of large language models. Frameworks such as Think-on-Graph and Graph CoT retrieve or identify relevant graph components and then conduct multi-step reasoning through graph interaction.

l: Chain-of-Thought, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: improves complex multi-hop reasoning [through prompting techniques] Chain-of-Thought prompting can improve performance and scalability, especially for complex multi-hop reasoning. GraphRAG methods extend it with graph evidence, although error accumulation remains a serious problem.

l: collaborative knowledge graph refinement, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a in-context learning technique [for optimizing LLM responses] Collaborative knowledge graph refinement improves model responses by using factual knowledge graphs to verify and refine initial outputs. It can also use model feedback to identify missing triples and enrich the knowledge graph.

l: domain-specific models, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: enhance multimodal information processing [through training with domain-specific models] Domain-specific models are used to improve large language models' handling of multimodal representations and domain-specific tasks. Fine-tuning with these models can improve generalization across domains while helping models use information that might otherwise appear as out-of-vocabulary tokens.

l: multi-round integration, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Multi-round integration iteratively refines retrieved content, generates intermediate reasoning, aligns outputs with target labels, and adds quality assurance for inconsistent retrieval and complex sequential questions.

l: multimodal information, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: reduces input lengths [when represented by learned image representations] Multimodal information, including image representations learned by vision-language models, can reduce input length while preserving rich information. Alignment techniques can fuse modalities, but large language models may have difficulty exploiting representations treated as out-of-vocabulary tokens.

l: hallucination, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: Hallucination is a risk in large language model responses. It is mitigated by grounding generation in retrieved factual knowledge, verifying and refining outputs with knowledge graphs, and filtering irrelevant or distracting retrieved content.

l: error accumulation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: is_a problem in CoT-based methods [during complex reasoning] Error accumulation is a severe problem in Chain-of-Thought-based knowledge integration, particularly when reasoning proceeds through multiple steps. Diversifying reasoning paths is proposed as a way to reduce the effects of error propagation.

l: generation, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: focuses_on large language model [for context-aware, accurate, and efficient content generation] Generation uses retrieved and inherent knowledge to produce responses through a large language model. The unit describes efforts to make generation more accurate and efficient through context filtering, self-reflection, compression, caching, and concurrent retrieval.

l: Freebase, A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models
s: supports SimpleQuestion [as its knowledge graph] Freebase provides the background knowledge for datasets and systems including SimpleQuestion, WebQ, CWQ, WebQSP, MetaQA, ToG, ToG 2.0, RoG, SubgraphRAG, SG-RAG, R-DP, GAIL, DialogGSR, and SURGE. It is used for direct fact retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, complex question answering, and movie- or dialogue-related applications.

l: RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models
s: This unit studies whether Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) makes large language models safer than non-RAG systems when responding to harmful questions. It defines RAG as a pipeline in which a retriever, such as BM25, selects relevant documents for an LLM to use alongside a user query, unlike non-RAG models that rely on stored knowledge and a different instruction. Across 5,592 harmful questions and eleven LLMs, evaluated with BM25 over English Wikipedia and Llama Guard 2, the study finds that RAG is generally not safer. Eight of eleven models show substantially changed safety behavior, often producing more unsafe responses; for Llama-3-8B, unsafe responses rise from 0.3% without RAG to 9.2% with RAG. RAG also changes risk profiles in model-dependent ways, with Llama-3-8B-Instruct becoming vulnerable in all 16 risk categories. The analysis examines inherent model safety, document safety, and models’ ability to perform RAG tasks. RAG retains many non-RAG vulnerabilities while adding new unsafe behavior, even where both the model and retrieved documents are safe. Unsafe documents increase risk, but most unsafe outputs come from safe documents, because models may repurpose retrieved information or add internal knowledge. Weak information extraction, refusal behavior, and incomplete attention to documents can further affect apparent and actual safety. The unit then tests red-teaming methods GCG and AutoDAN under access to the model and retriever but not the corpus. Jailbreak prompts optimized for non-RAG models usually do not transfer to RAG, though AutoDAN transfers somewhat better. Methods optimized directly for RAG can succeed on training data, but testing success falls when prompts retrieve different documents. The study concludes that RAG-specific red-teaming and aligned training/testing retrieval conditions are needed. It recommends RAG-tailored safety fine-tuning, re-retrieval during attack optimization, penalties for unstable retrieval, and prompts optimized across many documents. Limitations include the exclusion of RAG-trained LLMs such as Command R2, use of BM25 rather than dense retrievers, complex model-query-document interactions, and constraints involving red-teaming assumptions, risk definitions, user settings, and corpora. The paper acknowledges harmful generated language and possible misuse, while aiming to expose vulnerabilities and support safer models and defenses.

l: RAG, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models
s: RAG is a framework and model setting in which relevant documents are identified from a corpus and supplied as context for large language models (LLMs), which synthesize that material into responses. It is widely used, with popular strategies using documents alone or documents plus model knowledge. Its central importance is that grounding responses in source documents can reduce hallucinations and facilitate attributed generation, yet it can also change safety profiles: most LLMs in RAG settings show more unsafe responses than in non-RAG settings, even when both models and retrieved documents are safe. RAG can amplify existing unsafe behavior, introduce vulnerabilities across nearly every safety category, and become less safe with additional context; even one relevant document can alter safety behavior. In the evaluated system, BM25 retrieves five paragraph-level documents from an English Wikipedia corpus, under document-only and document-plus-knowledge settings. RAG-specific jailbreaking prompts are more effective than transferred prompts, though altering retrieval reduces their success. These vulnerabilities create distinct challenges for safety fine-tuning, red-teaming, and dynamic corpora.

Although they are aligned with human values through several development approaches and evaluated for safety, they remain susceptible to unsafe content. A comparative analysis of eleven LLMs examines safety in RAG and non-RAG frameworks, finding that safety can change with RAG and that most LLMs in the RAG setting show a higher percentage of unsafe responses. The study seeks to uncover overlooked RAG vulnerabilities.

l: retrieved documents, RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models

Documents may contain harmful information, be repurposed harmfully, or fail to constrain internal knowledge; unsafe generations can rise as context length increases, and risk differences across models sharing documents show documents alone do not explain unsafe responses. In training, five documents come from original queries; testing retrieves anew from optimized prompts, lowering attack success. s: RAG LLMs are language models that synthesize retrieved documents and therefore have safety requirements distinct from non-RAG models.
